title: The Power Of 'Just Reading' A Good Novel
author: Natalie Wexler
summary: Natalie Wexler argues that middle and high school English classes have drifted into teaching comprehension through short excerpts and close reading drills, driven by standardized-test pressure and a misreading of the Common Core. She cites an English study in which students who heard two whole challenging novels read aloud at pace gained nine months of reading progress, and weaker readers sixteen months, while added comprehension instruction made no difference. She adds her own classroom observations from the Bookworms curriculum in Delaware and from Michaela school in London, where read-aloud of demanding books holds students rapt and closes large reading gaps. Her interpretation is that volume of rich text, emotional engagement, vocabulary and syntax absorption, and higher teacher expectations matter more than skills drills. She acknowledges open questions about who should read aloud, and that students still need discussion and knowledge-building, but urges teachers to try spending less time on skills and more on a long, good story.
points: Test-prep pressure and a misreading of the Common Core's close reading have pushed secondary English toward fragments of text instead of whole books.
An English study found that reading whole challenging novels aloud at pace boosted comprehension substantially, while explicit comprehension instruction added nothing.
Emotional engagement with a story builds vocabulary and absorbs written syntax in ways decontextualized excerpts cannot.
Michaela and the Bookworms curriculum show read-aloud of demanding texts working for struggling readers, including those far below grade level.
Wexler suggests teachers spend less time on isolated skills and more on immersing students in long, rich books.
quotes: The tests aim to assess comprehension abilities through questions about short passages on disconnected topics, and teachers try to prepare their students by mimicking that approach in their instruction.

Coleman’s intent was to move teachers away from disconnected comprehension “skills” and toward immersing students in rich text. But many teachers got the opposite message, concluding that the Common Core was all about building skills, including "close reading.
Close reading of brief text has its place, and—done well—it can help students learn how to wrest meaning from complex text.

After getting through two novels in 12 weeks, average readers made a full nine months of progress. And poor readers made 16 months of progress. But the researchers were wrong about the value of comprehension instruction. It made no difference.

They may also unconsciously absorb more of the sophisticated syntax and conventions that appear only in written language, which can help them understand other complex text. Brief passages and decontextualized excerpts don't allow for the emotional engagement that reading a novel provides.

The practice of having the teacher read aloud while students follow along, and are occasionally called on to read a sentence or two, is used throughout the curriculum at Michaela. And it seems to work. The school takes in many students who are reading on the level of a six-year-old at the age of 11, but within two years they've all caught up to where they should be.

Clearly, students need to do more than just listen to novels to develop the fund of knowledge that will enable them to understand complex text in history, science, and other subjects. And English teachers need to lead some discussion of what's going on in a novel. But they might want to try spending less time on “skills” and more on just plunging into a good, long story.
